studies.title: Garlic extract favorably modifies markers of endothelial function in obese patients -randomized double blind placebo-controlled nutritional intervention.
studies.abstract: Garlic exerts a range of effects relevant to human health. However, its influence on the endothelium in obese individuals remains unknown. We aimed to determine the effects of garlic extract (GE) on arterial stiffness and markers of endothelial function. Ninety-two subjects were enrolled in this study. The participants were randomly assigned to receive 400 mg of GE or placebo daily for 3 months. The arterial stiffness index (SI) and markers of endothelial function such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), cholesterol (total, LDL, HDL), triglycerides, and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1), as well as total antioxidant status (TAS) were quantified at baseline and the end of study. At the end of study SI (p = 0.01), hsCRP (p < 0.001, PAI-1 (p < 0.001), LDL cholesterol (p < 0.001), and TAS (p < 0.01) were reduced in the GE-supplemented group, but not in the placebo group. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial demonstrates that supplementation with GE favorably modifies endothelial biomarkers associated with cardiovascular risk and suggests that GE can be used to suppress chronic inflammation in obese individuals.

studies.title: Aged garlic extract reduces blood pressure in hypertensives: a dose-response trial.
studies.abstract: Hypertension affects about 30% of adults worldwide. Garlic has blood pressure-lowering properties and the mechanism of action is biologically plausible. Our trial assessed the effect, dose-response, tolerability and acceptability of different doses of aged garlic extract as an adjunct treatment to existing antihypertensive medication in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. A total of 79 general practice patients with uncontrolled systolic hypertension participated in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled dose-response trial of 12 weeks. Participants were allocated to one of three garlic groups with either of one, two or four capsules daily of aged garlic extract (240/480/960 mg containing 0.6/1.2/2.4 mg of S-allylcysteine) or placebo. Blood pressure was assessed at 4, 8 and 12 weeks and compared with baseline using a mixed-model approach. Tolerability was monitored throughout the trial and acceptability was assessed at 12 weeks by questionnaire. Mean systolic blood pressure was significantly reduced by 11.8±5.4 mm Hg in the garlic-2-capsule group over 12 weeks compared with placebo (P=0.006), and reached borderline significant reduction in the garlic-4-capsule group at 8 weeks (-7.4±4.1 mm Hg, P=0.07). Changes in systolic blood pressure in the garlic-1-capsule group and diastolic blood pressure were not significantly different to placebo. Tolerability, compliance and acceptability were high in all garlic groups (93%) and highest in the groups taking one or two capsules daily. Our trial suggests aged garlic extract to be an effective and tolerable treatment in uncontrolled hypertension, and may be considered as a safe adjunct treatment to conventional antihypertensive therapy.

studies.title: Effects of anethum graveolens and garlic on lipid profile in hyperlipidemic patients.
studies.abstract: hyperlipidemia as a major risk factor of atherosclerosis is treated with different drugs. Concerning length of therapy and vast majority of side effects, herbal medication may be suitable substitute for these drugs. In this single-blind, placebo controlled study, lipid profiles of 150 hyperlipidemic patients in cardiology outpatient department of Shiraz University of Medical Sciences were checked at same conditions. They were divided into three equal groups randomly (each composing of 50 patients). They were given enteric-coated garlic powder tablet (equal to 400 mg garlic, 1 mg allicin) twice daily, anethum tablet (650 mg) twice daily, and placebo tablet. All patients were put on NCEP type Pi diet and Six weeks later, lipid profiles were checked. In garlic group: total cholesterol (decreased by 26.82 mg/dl, 12.1% reduction, and P-value: .000), and LDL-cholesterol (decreased by 22.18 mg/dl, 17.3% reduction, and P-value: .000) dropped. HDL-cholesterol (increased by 10.02 mg/dl, 15.7% increase, and P-value: .000) increased. Although triglyceride dropped by 13.72 mg/dl (6.3%) but this was not significant statistically (P-value: .222). In anethum group: surprisingly, triglyceride increased by 14.74 mg/dl (6.0%). Anethum could reduce total cholesterol by 0.4 % and LDL-cholesterol by 6.3% but these were not significant statistically (P-value: .828, and .210, respectively). Anethum has no significant effect on lipid profile, but garlic tablet has significant favorable effect on cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and HDL-cholesterol. Garlic may play an important role in therapy of hypercholesterolemia.

studies.title: Garlic extract therapy in children with hypercholesterolemia.
studies.abstract: To determine whether garlic extract therapy is efficacious and safe in children with hypercholesterolemia. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Specialized pediatric lipid disorders ambulatory clinic. Thirty pediatric patients, aged 8 to 18 years, who had familial hyperlipidemia and a minimum fasting total cholesterol level greater than 4.8 mmol/L (> 185 mg/dL). An 8-week course of a commercially available garlic extract (Kwai [Lichtwer Pharma, Berlin, Germany], 300 mg, 3 times a day) or an identical placebo. Absolute and relative changes in fasting lipid profile parameters. The groups were equivalent at baseline and compliance was similar in the 2 groups (P = .45). There was no significant relative attributable effect of garlic extract on fasting total cholesterol (+0.6% [95% confidence interval, -5.8% to +6.9%1) or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-0.5% [95% confidence interval, -8.7% to +7.6%]). The lower limits of the confidence intervals did not include -10%, the minimum relative attributable effect believed to be clinically important. Likewise, no significant effect was seen on the levels of high-density lipoprotein, triglycerides, apolipoprotein B-100, lipoprotein (a), fibrinogen, homocysteine, or blood pressure. There was a small effect on apolipoprotein A-I (+10.0% [95% confidence interval, +1.2% to +16.5%] P=.03). There were no differences in adverse effects between groups. Garlic extract therapy has no significant effect on cardiovascular risk factors in pediatric patients with familial hyperlipidemia.

studies.title: Effect of the essential oils of garlic and onion on alimentary hyperlipemia.
studies.abstract: The effect of garlic and onion on alimentary hyperlipemia, induced by feeding 100 g butter, has been studied in 10 healthy subjects. The freshly extracted juice of 50 g of garlic or onion, as well as an equivalent amount of their ether-extracted essential oils, was administered randomly on four different days during a one-week period. Garlic and onion have a significant protective action against fat-induced increases in serum cholesterol and plasma fibrinogen and decreases in coagulation time and fibrinolytic activity. The essential oil fraction, which contains all the taste and odour, exactly duplicated the beneficial effects of whole garlic and onion. It is, therefore, concluded that the active principle of garlic and onion is the essential oil, which chemically is a combination of sulphur-containing compounds, mainly allyl propyl disulphide and diallyl disulphide.

studies.title: Aged Garlic Extract Attenuates CaCl<sub>2</sub>-Induced Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Formation by Inhibiting Matrix Metalloproteinase 9 Expression in M
studies.abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a local enlargement of the abdominal aorta with the risk of its fatal rupture. With lack of established medical treatments reducing the AAA growth, the development of treatment strategies for AAA is warranted. In this study, we examined whether aged garlic extract (AGE), which reportedly has vasoprotective effects, attenuates AAA formation in an animal model. AAAs were induced via CaCl<sub>2</sub> application to the abdominal aortas of C57BL/6J mice. The intake of an AGE-containing diet attenuated the aortic dilatation after AAA induction. Histological analysis showed that the degradation of elastic fibers in AAAs was mild in mice fed AGE compared to that in control mice. In addition, the expression of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9), a proteolytic enzyme degrading aortic tissue, was decreased in AAAs from mice fed with AGE. In cultured macrophages, AGE significantly inhibited tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α-induced Mmp9 mRNA expression. Furthermore, AGE attenuated TNF-α-induced extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation and c-fos mRNA expression, suggesting the suppressive effect of AGE on ERK-c-Fos-MMP9 axis induced by TNF-α. The present findings indicate that AGE diminishes AAA formation by mitigating tissue destruction, highlighting the potential cardiovascular benefits of AGE intake.

studies.title: Effect of Garlic Extract on the Erythrocyte as a Simple Model Cell.
studies.abstract: Garlic is known to have diverse effects on mammalian cells, being cytotoxic, especially to cancer cells, but also protect against oxidative stress. Mammalian erythrocyte is a simple cell devoid of intracellular organelles, protein synthesis ability, and most signaling pathways. Therefore, examination of the effects of garlic on erythrocytes allows for revealing primary events in the cellular action of garlic extract. In this study, human erythrocytes or erythrocyte membranes were exposed to garlic extract at various dilutions. Hemoglobin oxidation to methemoglobin, increased binding of hemoglobin to the membrane, and formation of Heinz bodies were observed. Garlic extract depleted acid-soluble thiols, especially glutathione, and induced a prooxidative shift in the cellular glutathione redox potential. The extract increased the osmotic fragility of erythrocytes, induced hemolysis, and inhibited hemolysis in isotonic ammonium chloride, indicative of decreased membrane permeability for Cl<sup>-</sup> and increased the membrane fluidity. Fluorescent probes indicated an increased level of reactive oxygen species and induction of lipid peroxidation, but these results should be interpreted with care since the extract alone induced oxidation of the probes (dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate and BODIPY C11). These results demonstrate that garlic extract induces oxidative changes in the erythrocyte, first of all, thiol and hemoglobin oxidation.

studies.title: A combination of silymarin and garlic extract enhances thyroid hormone activation and body metabolism in orally intoxicated male rats with atrazine: Impact on h
studies.abstract: Atrazine is a widely applied herbicide to improve crop yield and maintain general health. It has been reported to impair thyroid function and architecture in experimental animals. Alterations in thyroid hormones disrupt normal body function and metabolism. Silymarin, a hepatoprotective flavonolignan, was found to improve thyroid function and body metabolism. Additionally, garlic displays several protective effects on body organs. Therefore, this study explored the prophylactic impact of natural compounds comprising silymarin and garlic extract on disrupted thyroid function, hepatic iodothyronine deiodinase type 1, and metabolic parameters in atrazine-intoxicated male rats. We found that daily pre- and co-treatment of atrazine-intoxicated male rats with silymarin (100 mg/kg, p.o) and/or garlic extract (10 mg/kg, p.o) significantly improved thyroid activation and hepatic functionality as evidenced by the re-establishment of T3, T3/T4, and TSH values as well as ALT and AST activities. Interestingly, individual or concurrent supplementation of the atrazine group with silymarin and garlic extract prevented the down-regulation in hepatic iodothyronine deiodinase type 1. These effects were coupled with the repletion of serum and hepatic antioxidants and the amelioration of lipid peroxidation. In addition, current natural products markedly alleviated weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance. Notably, a cocktail of silymarin and garlic extract exerted superior protection against atrazine-triggered deterioration of thyroid, hepatic, and metabolic functioning to individual treatments. Present findings pinpoint the prophylactic and synergistic influence of silymarin and garlic extract combinatorial regimen on thyroid activation and body metabolism via enhancing antioxidant potential, maintaining hepatic function, and iodothyronine deiodinase type 1.

studies.title: The possible alleviating effect of garlic supplement on the neural retina in a rat model of hypercholesterolemia: a histological and immunohistochemical study.
studies.abstract: The purpose of this work was to prove that oxidative stress is the main mechanism responsible for retinal neurodegenerative changes, subsequent apoptosis, and inflammatory cytokine release in rats fed with a high cholesterol diet (HCD) and determine the role of garlic in alleviating these changes. Forty rats were equally divided into four groups: control, garlic-treated (positive control), HCD, and HCD + garlic-treated (HCD + G). By the end of the experiment (24 weeks) blood samples were collected for assessment of serum lipid profile, oxidative stress parameters, and plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF-α. Both eyes of the rats were enucleated; one was used for light microscopic examination and the other for electron microscopic examination. There was a significant increase in the levels of serum lipids, oxidative stress parameters, IL-6 and TNF-α, and area of expression of caspase-3 in the HCD group compared to both the control and HCD + G groups. Histological examination revealed degenerative changes in all layers of the neural retina in the HCD group. Garlic administration resulted in a significant improvement in the biochemical, immunohistochemical, and histological characteristics of hypercholesterolemic rats. These findings support the hypotheses that garlic has strong antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties. Garlic ameliorates the neurodegenerative changes in the neural retina of hypercholesteremic rats.

studies.title: The potential effect of garlic extract and curcumin nanoparticles against complication accompanied with experimentally induced diabetes in rats.
studies.abstract: Modified herbal medicines implicate the combination of several therapeutic practices of native systems of medicine that may extend many earlier generations, which frequently afford valuable therapeutic benefits. In this study, the role of nano-curcumin and aged garlic extract (AGE) as two modified phytomedicines on alleviating both of advanced glycation end products (AGEPs) and oxidative stress (OS) in streptozotocin (STZ) induced diabetic rats were investigated during this study. Nano-curcumin and AGE suspension were orally administrated at a dose of 300, 500 mg/kg body weight respectively. Serum glucose, insulin, total cholesterol, triglycerides and myocardial enzyme activities including creatine kinase-isoenzyme (CK-MB), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) were determined biochemically, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR)-test had been used to determine relative of manganese-superoxide dismutase (Mn-SOD) and receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) gene expressions in the heart tissue of rats. Structure of rat's heart tissue was examined by histopathological analysis (H&E). AGE increased the body weight and insulin concentration, while, it decreased serum glucose concentration, CK-MB, and LDH enzyme activities in comparing with the diabetic group. In addition, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and AST didn't show any significant changes in serum values of AGE compared to diabetic rats. Nano-curcumin suspension decreased the serum levels of triglycerides, CK- MB, LDH, and AST. While, there were non-significant changes in the body weight, glucose, insulin, and total cholesterol level of the same group compared with the STZ- untreated induced diabetic rats. The transcript quantity of manganese-superoxide dismutase gene (Mn-SOD) was highly accumulated (3.25 and 3.87-fold) in the heart tissue sample of the induced diabetic rats in response to both nano-Curcumin and AGE suspension respectively. While AGE was the most potent treatment where it caused down regulation of the receptor for advanced glycation end products gene (RAGE) expression (1.79-fold). Results of histopathological analyses under the light microscope showed restoring the structural integrity of the myocytes towards normalization in diabetic hearts treated with each of nano-curcumin and AGE suspension compared with the untreated diabetic heart samples. Nano-curcumin and AGE suspension have a great therapeutic potential in the treatment of DCM, Diabetic cardiomyopathy, by attenuating cardiac inflammation, myocardial fibrosis, and programmed myocardial cell deaths through inhibiting OS and AGEPs accumulation in diabetic heart tissue. Furthermore, the hypoglycemic antioxidant properties of AGE resulted in more potent therapeutic effect than nano-curcumin in the treatment of diabetic hearts.

studies.title: Antiobesity Effect of Garlic Extract Fermented by Lactobacillus plantarum BL2 in Diet-Induced Obese Mice.
studies.abstract: Obesity is viewed as a serious public health problem. This study aimed to investigate the antiobesity effects of fermented garlic extract by lactic acid bacteria (LAFGE) on obesity. Male C57BL/6J mice were fed with high-fat diet (HFD) to induce obesity. The HFD-induced obese mice were orally administrated with 250 or 500 mg/kg LAFGE for 8 weeks. Feeding HFD-fed mice with 250 or 500 mg/kg LAFGE reduced body weight by 14% and 18%, respectively, compared to HFD. HFD-fed mice with 500 mg/kg LAFGE administration had lower epididymal, retroperitoneal, and mesenteric adipose tissue mass by 36%, 44%, and 63%, respectively, compared to HFD. The concentration of plasma triacylglyceride and total cholesterol was significantly lower in the HFD-fed mice with LAFGE administration. Moreover, LAFGE supplementation suppressed adipogenesis by downregulation in mRNA and protein expression of PPARγ, C/EBPα, and lipogenic proteins, including SREBP-1c, FAS, and SCD-1. Based on these findings, LAFGE may ameliorate diet-induced obesity by inhibiting adipose tissue hypertrophy by suppressing adipogenesis.

studies.title: Effect of garlic extract on blood glucose level and lipid profile in normal and alloxan diabetic rabbits.
studies.abstract: Comparative hypoglycemic and hypolipidaemic activity of garlic (ethanol) extract and metformin was the aim of the study in 24 normal and diabetic rabbits. In group A of 12 rabbits, the influence of different doses (250, 300 and 350 mg/kg body weight) of garlic extract was evaluated, six of them were kept normal, while six were caused to be diabetic with alloxan (150 mg/kg body weight). In another group B of 12 rabbits, the influence of various doses of metformin (250, 375 and 500 mg/kg body weight) was also assessed in the similar grouping of six normal and six diabetic rabbits. The maximum hypoglycemic response was observed with highest doses of garlic extract (350 mg/kg body weight) in normal rabbits 4 h after garlic extract administration, while in diabetic rabbits, blood glucose level (270.3 ± 0.8 mg/dl) was significantly (p < 0.05) lowered as compared to the control level (303.8 ± 1.8 mg/dl). The levels of triglycerides (44.0 ± 0.9 mg/dl) and cholesterol (32.8 ± 0.7 mg/dl) also significantly (p < 0.05) decreased in normal rabbits after 4 h of extract administration as compared to that of 0 h samples (triglycerides 66.0 ± 1.5 mg/dl and cholesterol 47.5 ± 0.5 mg/dl). In diabetic rabbits, 0 h level of triglyceride and cholesterol was found to be 86.5 ± 1.1 mg/dl and 93.8 ± 0.9 mg/dl, respectively and levels seen in 4 h sample were 61.3 ± 1.2 mg/dl and 57.0 ± 1.8 mg/dl, respectively. In normal as well as diabetic rabbits, garlic extract produced hypoglycemia as well as hypolipidaemia like metformin, but the hypoglycemic effect was more pronounced with metformin, whereas garlic extract was more effective in causing hypolipidaemia as compared to metformin.

studies.title: Study of garlic extracts and fractions on cholesterol plasma levels and vascular reactivity in cholesterol-fed rats.
studies.abstract: Garlic is known for its pharmacologic and nutritional properties. In previous studies, garlic elicited a reduction in plasma levels of lipids by inhibiting hepatic cholesterol synthesis. The aim of this study was to investigate in an in vivo model the effects of garlic extract and some fractions on cholesterol levels and vascular reactivity in cholesterol-fed rats. Rats were fed a cholesterol-enriched diet for 16 wk and were divided into 10 groups as follows: control and hypercholesterolemic diet groups, 4 groups fed frozen garlic fractions and 4 groups fed raw garlic fractions with different doses. Blood samples were obtained to analyze HDL and LDL cholesterol levels. After treatment, rats were killed. The heart, liver and kidneys were weighed; the aorta was isolated, mounted in organ chambers and vascular reactivity was tested. Plasma concentration of cholesterol was 58 mg/dL (100%) at the beginning of the study and increased to 102 mg/dL (153%; hypercholesterolemic group) at the end of the treatment. Plasma total cholesterol decreased in all groups treated with garlic; moreover, this effect was higher in rats fed raw garlic fractions and extracts. LDL decreased significantly with respect to the hypercholesterolemic group in all groups treated with garlic fractions and extracts (P: < 0.01); however, an increase in HDL was found in those treated with frozen fractions and extracts. The liver:body weight ratio decreased in all treated groups. The relaxing effect of acetylcholine (ACh) was enhanced in arteries contracted with noradrenaline (NE). These data suggest that garlic fractions could prevent diet-induced hypercholesterolemia and vascular alterations in the endothelium-dependent relaxation associated with atherosclerosis.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A concentrate of garlic bulbs, usually standardized and dried, taken as capsules or powder.
explanation.what_it_is: Garlic extract is made by concentrating compounds from garlic bulbs (Allium sativum), often freeze-dried or processed to preserve active molecules like allicin and other sulfur compounds. It comes as capsules, powders, or aged extracts (where garlic is fermented to reduce odor and change its chemistry). People take it as a supplement, typically in doses of 600–1,500 mg per day, to target heart health and immunity.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Contains sulfur compounds that reduce inflammation, relax blood vessels, and may modulate immune cell activity.
explanation.how_it_works: Garlic extract contains a family of molecules built around sulfur — the most famous is allicin, which forms when garlic cells are crushed. These sulfur compounds appear to work through several paths: they can relax the smooth muscle in blood vessel walls (similar to how some blood pressure drugs work), reduce stiffness in arteries, and dampen inflammatory signals that drive atherosclerosis (hardening of arteries). Animal studies suggest garlic compounds also activate immune cells and reduce oxidative stress (a type of cellular damage). The exact human mechanism for these effects remains incompletely understood, but the compounds' anti-inflammatory and vessel-relaxing properties are well-documented in laboratory and animal models.
explanation.safety_line: Mild GI effects reported in trials; long-term safety and effects in specific populations remain understudied.
explanation.safety_detail: The trials retrieved reported garlic extract to be generally well-tolerated, with the most common side effects being mild gastrointestinal symptoms (stomach upset, odor) and occasional headache. However, most retrieved studies were short-term (weeks to a few months), and detailed safety monitoring in vulnerable groups — such as people on blood-thinning drugs, those with kidney disease, or pregnant women — was not adequately represented in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: garlic may potentiate blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin); concurrent use untested in retrieved trials.
Pregnancy and lactation: excluded from nearly all trials; safety unknown.
Long-term use: studies retrieved were typically 8–12 weeks; effects beyond 6 months not established in provided records.
explanation.chem_meaning: Garlic extract is rich in small, polar sulfur-containing molecules (like allicin and diallyl disulfide) that dissolve in water and body fluids, allowing them to be absorbed through the digestive tract and distributed in the bloodstream. These compounds are volatile (they evaporate, creating garlic's smell) and reactive, which is why processing methods (aging, drying, standardization) significantly alter their chemistry and bioactivity.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies — including meta-analyses from 2020 (n=374), 2016 (n=2,300), 2015, and a comprehensive 2026 systematic review (n=7,137) — found that garlic extract lowered blood pressure in people with hypertension. The pooled average reduction was approximately 3.75 mmHg (range −5.04 to −2.45), a modest but consistent effect. Recent trials from 2024–2025 on aged garlic and freeze-dried extracts confirmed improved cardiovascular markers including aerobic fitness.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects that evidence is human-based and consistent across multiple meta-analyses, but the absolute number of independent primary trials (4) is below the threshold for strong evidence. The effect size is small to moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twelve human studies (6 primary trials and 6 meta-analyses), encompassing over 11,000 verified participants across the studies that reported sample size, examined garlic extract's effect on lipid profiles. Meta-analyses spanning 1993–2021, including a 2016 analysis of 2,300 people and a 2009 analysis of 1,056 participants, found modest reductions in serum cholesterol. The pooled effect was very small (mean difference −0.04 mmol/L, range −0.15 to 0.07), suggesting a weak or inconsistent lipid-lowering effect. Six animal studies also showed reductions in blood lipids, but human efficacy was more modest than animal data.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects human evidence and consistency across decades of meta-analyses, but the pooled effect is tiny and confidence intervals cross zero, meaning the true effect may be negligible. Only 6 primary human studies were retrieved; the lipid effect is less robust than blood pressure findings.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (1 primary trial and 2 analyses, totaling ~2,550 verified participants in those reporting sample size) addressed immune outcomes. A 2016 meta-analysis of 2,300 people reported garlic stimulated immunity. A 2006 RCT examined garlic's effect on precancerous gastric lesions via immune-related mechanisms. A 2022 systematic review summarized immune findings. Seven animal studies (2024–2026) demonstrated anti-parasitic activity, infection resistance, and immune cell activation in fish and invertebrate models, but these do not directly establish human immune benefits.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects that human immune data are sparse (only 1 primary trial retrieved) compared to animal evidence. The grade acknowledges promising mechanistic data but recognizes that human immune outcomes have not been studied as rigorously as blood pressure. Evidence is suggestive rather than definitive.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fourteen human studies (7 primary trials and 7 meta-analyses, ~11,120 verified participants across those reporting size) assessed broad cardiovascular outcomes including blood pressure, lipids, arterial stiffness, and coronary artery disease risk. Large meta-analyses from 2016 (n=2,300), 2020 (n=374), 2009 (n=1,056), and a 2026 systematic review (n=7,137) consistently found modest reductions in blood pressure and cholesterol. A 2021 meta-analysis focused on patients with established coronary artery disease. Eight animal studies supported anti-atherosclerotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. The pooled blood pressure effect (used as a proxy for cardiovascular benefit) was −3.75 mmHg.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects that cardiovascular outcomes are primarily driven by modest improvements in blood pressure; lipid effects are weak. Human evidence is substantial in volume (14 studies across decades) but mostly from meta-analyses of small trials. Seven primary human trials is below the threshold for strong evidence. The effect is real but clinically small.

explanation.evidence_base: Evidence is predominantly human (33 human studies vs. 15 animal studies retrieved) and dominated by meta-analyses and systematic reviews spanning 1993–2026, which pool data from many smaller trials. The largest studies are meta-analyses (up to n=7,137 for the 2026 cardiovascular review). This means the base comes from many small, older trials rather than a few large modern RCTs. Recency is mixed: some meta-analyses are decades old (1993), but recent systematic reviews (2024–2026) have updated findings. This pattern suggests modest, consistent effects that have been repeatedly observed, but individual trials remain limited in size and rigor.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show that blood pressure is the best-studied outcome (eight human studies), while immune function is the least studied (only one primary trial). Durations are typically short (8–12 weeks); whether benefits persist or accumulate over months or years is not addressed in the provided records. Comparisons between extract types (aged vs. fresh, standardized vs. non-standardized) are absent from the summaries given. Adolescent, pregnant, and kidney-disease populations do not appear in any retrieved trials, so effects in these groups are entirely unknown.

appraisal.headline: Blood pressure shows a modest pooled reduction (-3.75 mmHg), but the cholesterol effect is null (pooled CI crosses zero), and immune function evidence is predominantly animal studies with only 1 primary human RCT—claims should be sized to match the actual evidence.

concerns.detail: The pooled effect for cholesterol/lipids is -0.04 mmol/L with 95% CI [-0.15 to 0.07]—a confidence interval that crosses zero. This indicates no statistically significant effect on lipid profiles. Yet 'Moderate' grading and the 2016 and 2020 meta-analyses titles claim garlic 'regulates serum cholesterol.' A reader may infer efficacy where the pooled data show none.

concerns.issue: Immune function: 70% of evidence is animal studies
concerns.detail: Of 10 immune function records, only 1 is a human RCT (2006); 5 are pure animal studies and 2 are unclassified (likely animal). The single meta-analysis contributing human data (2016, n=2300) is shared across other outcomes and no separate pooled effect is reported for immune outcomes. Grading this 'Moderate' misrepresents the evidence base as primarily preclinical.

concerns.issue: Primary RCT sample sizes are small and variable
concerns.detail: For blood pressure, the 4 primary RCTs report n = [49, 75, 79, 374]. Three of four are under 80 participants. For cardiovascular outcomes, 7 primary RCTs show similar range [49, 50, 75, 79]. A single outlier (e.g., the n=374 study) or differential dropout could meaningfully shift pooled estimates. Meta-analyses are present but rely on this small primary evidence base.

concerns.issue: Heterogeneity in garlic formulation and dosing not transparent
concerns.detail: Records include 'Kyolic aged garlic extract,' 'freeze-dried garlic extract,' and unspecified 'garlic extract'—at least three distinct formulations. Abstracts do not report dosing or treatment duration. Pooled effects may mask efficacy differences across formulation types, or conflate active and inactive preparations.

concerns.issue: Publication bias and meta-analysis quality not assessed in records
concerns.detail: Five meta-analyses and one systematic review are retrieved, but none of the records report funnel plots, Begg's test, Egger's test, or GRADE certainty assessments. The 1993 meta-analysis on cholesterol is 33 years old and predates modern search standards. No assessment of whether negative or small studies were systematically omitted.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Garlic's sulfur compounds (allicin, S-allylcysteine) are proposed to reduce oxidative stress and improve endothelial function—a plausible pathway to lower blood pressure and improve lipid profiles. However, the clinical evidence does not uniformly support this: blood pressure shows a modest but consistent reduction (−3.75 mmHg, 95% CI −5.04 to −2.45), but the cholesterol effect is null (CI crosses zero), which is discordant with a unified antioxidant mechanism. For immune function, the mechanism is more speculative and rests almost entirely on animal data, creating a large inferential gap from mechanistic studies to clinical benefit claims.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that the blood pressure effect of −3.75 mmHg is clinically marginal (equivalent to a single dietary change or minimal weight loss) and the confidence interval is narrow only because of pooling; individual RCTs are small and heterogeneous in design and populations. More tellingly, if garlic extract worked via a general antioxidant or lipid-lowering mechanism, cholesterol should improve—it does not (pooled CI includes zero). The immune function claim rests on 5 animal and 2 unclassified studies; the single human RCT (2006) assessed gastric lesion precancerosis, not immune markers. A well-informed skeptic would conclude the evidence supports a small, possibly clinically negligible blood pressure reduction in hypertensives, with no effect on cholesterol and no credible human evidence for immune enhancement.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: For blood pressure: a large (n ≥ 500), long-term (≥12 weeks) RCT in a representative hypertensive population with preregistration and assessment of heterogeneity by age, baseline BP, and garlic formulation. For cholesterol: the same design applied prospectively to lipid-lowering claims, since current pooled evidence is null. For immune function: replacement of the 70% animal evidence with adequately powered (n ≥ 200) human RCTs measuring validated immune endpoints (e.g., infection rates, antibody response) rather than in vitro markers.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un concentrado de bulbos de ajo, generalmente estandarizado y deshidratado, tomado en cápsulas o polvo.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El extracto de ajo se elabora concentrando compuestos de bulbos de ajo (Allium sativum), frecuentemente liofilizados o procesados para preservar moléculas activas como la alicina y otros compuestos de azufre. Se presenta en cápsulas, polvos o extractos envejecidos (donde el ajo se fermenta para reducir el olor y cambiar su química). Las personas lo toman como suplemento, típicamente en dosis de 600–1.500 mg por día, para mejorar la salud cardiovascular e inmunológica.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Contiene compuestos de azufre que reducen la inflamación, relajan los vasos sanguíneos y podrían modular la actividad de células inmunitarias.
explanation_es.how_it_works: El extracto de ajo contiene una familia de moléculas basadas en azufre, siendo la más famosa la alicina, que se forma cuando se machaca el ajo. Estos compuestos de azufre parecen actuar a través de varios mecanismos: pueden relajar el músculo liso en las paredes de los vasos sanguíneos (similar a cómo actúan algunos fármacos para la presión arterial), reducir la rigidez en las arterias y disminuir las señales inflamatorias que impulsan la aterosclerosis (endurecimiento de las arterias). Los estudios en animales sugieren que los compuestos del ajo también activan células inmunitarias y reducen el estrés oxidativo (un tipo de daño celular). El mecanismo exacto en humanos para estos efectos sigue siendo incompletamente comprendido, pero las propiedades antiinflamatorias y relajantes de los vasos de estos compuestos están bien documentadas en modelos de laboratorio y animales.
explanation_es.safety_line: Se reportan efectos gastrointestinales leves en ensayos; la seguridad a largo plazo y los efectos en poblaciones específicas siguen siendo poco estudiados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos recuperados reportaron que el extracto de ajo es generalmente bien tolerado, siendo los efectos secundarios más comunes síntomas gastrointestinales leves (malestar estomacal, olor) y ocasionalmente dolores de cabeza. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los estudios recuperados fueron de corta duración (semanas a pocos meses), y la monitorización detallada de seguridad en grupos vulnerables — como personas que toman anticoagulantes, aquellos con enfermedad renal o mujeres embarazadas — no estuvo adecuadamente representada en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Interacciones medicamentosas: el ajo puede potenciar anticoagulantes (warfarina, aspirina); el uso concurrente no ha sido probado en los ensayos recuperados.
Embarazo y lactancia: excluidos de casi todos los ensayos; la seguridad es desconocida.
Uso a largo plazo: los estudios recuperados fueron típicamente de 8–12 semanas; los efectos más allá de 6 meses no están establecidos en los registros proporcionados.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El extracto de ajo es rico en pequeñas moléculas polares que contienen azufre (como la alicina y el disulfuro de dialilo) que se disuelven en agua y líquidos corporales, permitiendo su absorción a través del tracto digestivo y distribución en el torrente sanguíneo. Estos compuestos son volátiles (se evaporan, creando el olor del ajo) y reactivos, por lo que los métodos de procesamiento (envejecimiento, secado, estandarización) alteran significativamente su química y bioactividad.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ocho estudios humanos — incluyendo metanálisis de 2020 (n=374), 2016 (n=2.300), 2015 y una revisión sistemática exhaustiva de 2026 (n=7.137) — encontraron que el extracto de ajo redujo la presión arterial en personas con hipertensión. La reducción promedio agrupada fue aproximadamente 3,75 mmHg (rango −5,04 a −2,45), un efecto modesto pero consistente. Ensayos recientes de 2024–2025 sobre ajo envejecido y extractos liofilizados confirmaron marcadores cardiovasculares mejorados incluyendo capacidad aeróbica.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja que la evidencia es basada en humanos y consistente a través de múltiples metanálisis, pero el número absoluto de ensayos primarios independientes (4) está por debajo del umbral para evidencia fuerte. El tamaño del efecto es pequeño a moderado.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Doce estudios humanos (6 ensayos primarios y 6 metanálisis), que abarcan más de 11.000 participantes verificados en los estudios que reportaron tamaño de muestra, examinaron el efecto del extracto de ajo en perfiles de lípidos. Metanálisis que abarcan 1993–2021, incluyendo un análisis de 2016 de 2.300 personas y un análisis de 2009 de 1.056 participantes, encontraron reducciones modestas en el colesterol sérico. El efecto agrupado fue muy pequeño (diferencia media −0,04 mmol/L, rango −0,15 a 0,07), sugiriendo un efecto reductor de lípidos débil o inconsistente. Seis estudios en animales también mostraron reducciones en lípidos sanguíneos, pero la eficacia humana fue más modesta que los datos en animales.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja evidencia humana y consistencia a través de décadas de metanálisis, pero el efecto agrupado es minúsculo e intervalos de confianza cruzan cero, significando que el efecto verdadero puede ser negligible. Solo 6 estudios primarios humanos fueron recuperados; el efecto de lípidos es menos robusto que los hallazgos de presión arterial.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres estudios humanos (1 ensayo primario y 2 análisis, totalizando ~2.550 participantes verificados en aquellos que reportaron tamaño de muestra) abordaron desenlaces inmunitarios. Un metanálisis de 2016 de 2.300 personas reportó que el ajo estimuló la inmunidad. Un ensayo controlado aleatorizado de 2006 examinó el efecto del ajo en lesiones gástricas precancerosas a través de mecanismos relacionados con inmunidad. Una revisión sistemática de 2022 resumió hallazgos inmunitarios. Siete estudios en animales (2024–2026) demostraron actividad antiparasitaria, resistencia a infecciones y activación de células inmunitarias en modelos de peces e invertebrados, pero estos no establecen directamente beneficios inmunitarios en humanos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja que los datos inmunitarios humanos son escasos (solo 1 ensayo primario recuperado) comparado con evidencia en animales. La calificación reconoce datos mecanísticos prometedores pero reconoce que los desenlaces inmunitarios humanos no han sido estudiados tan rigurosamente como la presión arterial. La evidencia es sugestiva más que definitiva.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Catorce estudios humanos (7 ensayos primarios y 7 metanálisis, ~11.120 participantes verificados en aquellos que reportaron tamaño) evaluaron amplios desenlaces cardiovasculares incluyendo presión arterial, lípidos, rigidez arterial y riesgo de enfermedad arterial coronaria. Grandes metanálisis de 2016 (n=2.300), 2020 (n=374), 2009 (n=1.056) y una revisión sistemática de 2026 (n=7.137) consistentemente encontraron reducciones modestas en presión arterial y colesterol. Un metanálisis de 2021 se enfocó en pacientes con enfermedad arterial coronaria establecida. Ocho estudios en animales apoyaron mecanismos antiateroscleróticos y antiinflamatorios. El efecto de presión arterial agrupado (usado como aproximación para beneficio cardiovascular) fue −3,75 mmHg.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja que los desenlaces cardiovasculares son principalmente impulsados por mejoras modestas en presión arterial; los efectos en lípidos son débiles. La evidencia humana es sustancial en volumen (14 estudios a través de décadas) pero mayormente de metanálisis de ensayos pequeños. Siete ensayos primarios humanos está por debajo del umbral para evidencia fuerte. El efecto es real pero clínicamente pequeño.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia es predominantemente humana (33 estudios humanos vs. 15 estudios en animales recuperados) y dominada por metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas que abarcan 1993–2026, que agrupan datos de muchos ensayos más pequeños. Los estudios más grandes son metanálisis (hasta n=7.137 para la revisión cardiovascular de 2026). Esto significa que la base proviene de muchos ensayos pequeños y antiguos más que de algunos ensayos controlados aleatorizados modernos grandes. La recencia es mixta: algunos metanálisis son de décadas atrás (1993), pero revisiones sistemáticas recientes (2024–2026) han actualizado los hallazgos. Este patrón sugiere efectos modestos y consistentes que han sido repetidamente observados, pero los ensayos individuales siguen siendo limitados en tamaño y rigor.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados muestran que la presión arterial es el desenlace mejor estudiado (ocho estudios humanos), mientras que la función inmunitaria es la menos estudiada (solo un ensayo primario). Las duraciones son típicamente cortas (8–12 semanas); si los beneficios persisten o se acumulan a lo largo de meses o años no es abordado en los registros proporcionados. Las comparaciones entre tipos de extracto (envejecido vs. fresco, estandarizado vs. no estandarizado) están ausentes de los resúmenes dados. Las poblaciones adolescente, embarazada y con enfermedad renal no aparecen en ningún ensayo recuperado, por lo que los efectos en estos grupos son completamente desconocidos.

appraisal_es.headline: La presión arterial muestra una reducción agrupada modesta (-3,75 mmHg), pero el efecto sobre el colesterol es nulo (IC agrupado cruza cero), y la evidencia de función inmunológica proviene predominantemente de estudios en animales con solo 1 ECA primario en humanos—las afirmaciones deben ajustarse al tamaño de la evidencia real.

concerns.issue: El efecto agrupado en colesterol es nulo
concerns.detail: El efecto agrupado para colesterol/lípidos es -0,04 mmol/L con IC 95% [-0,15 a 0,07]—un intervalo de confianza que cruza cero. Esto indica ningún efecto estadísticamente significativo en los perfiles lipídicos. Sin embargo, la calificación 'Moderada' y los títulos de los metanálisis de 2016 y 2020 afirman que el ajo 'regula el colesterol sérico.' Un lector podría inferir eficacia donde los datos agrupados no muestran ninguna.

concerns.issue: Función inmunológica: 70% de la evidencia proviene de estudios en animales
concerns.detail: De 10 registros de función inmunológica, solo 1 es un ECA en humanos (2006); 5 son estudios puros en animales y 2 no están clasificados (probablemente animales). El único metanálisis que contribuye datos en humanos (2016, n=2300) se comparte entre otros resultados y no se informa ningún efecto agrupado separado para resultados inmunológicos. Calificar esto como 'Moderado' tergiversa la base de evidencia como predominantemente preclínica.

concerns.issue: Los tamaños de muestra de los ECA primarios son pequeños y variables
concerns.detail: Para presión arterial, los 4 ECA primarios reportan n = [49, 75, 79, 374]. Tres de cuatro tienen menos de 80 participantes. Para resultados cardiovasculares, 7 ECA primarios muestran rango similar [49, 50, 75, 79]. Un único valor atípico (p. ej., el estudio n=374) o pérdida diferencial de participantes podrían cambiar significativamente las estimaciones agrupadas. Existen metanálisis pero se basan en esta pequeña base de evidencia primaria.

concerns.issue: La heterogeneidad en la formulación y dosificación del ajo no es transparente
concerns.detail: Los registros incluyen 'extracto de ajo envejecido Kyolic,' 'extracto de ajo liofilizado' y 'extracto de ajo' no especificado—al menos tres formulaciones distintas. Los resúmenes no reportan dosificación o duración del tratamiento. Los efectos agrupados pueden enmascarar diferencias de eficacia entre tipos de formulación, o confundir preparaciones activas e inactivas.

concerns.issue: Sesgo de publicación y calidad del metanálisis no evaluados en los registros
concerns.detail: Se recuperaron cinco metanálisis y una revisión sistemática, pero ninguno de los registros reporta gráficos de embudo, prueba de Begg, prueba de Egger, o evaluaciones de certeza GRADE. El metanálisis de 1993 sobre colesterol tiene 33 años y es anterior a los estándares de búsqueda modernos. No hay evaluación de si los estudios negativos o pequeños fueron sistemáticamente omitidos.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: Los compuestos de azufre del ajo (alicina, S-alilcisteína) se proponen para reducir el estrés oxidativo y mejorar la función endotelial—un mecanismo plausible para reducir la presión arterial y mejorar los perfiles lipídicos. Sin embargo, la evidencia clínica no lo apoya uniformemente: la presión arterial muestra una reducción modesta pero consistente (-3,75 mmHg, IC 95% -5,04 a -2,45), pero el efecto sobre colesterol es nulo (IC cruza cero), lo cual es discordante con un mecanismo antioxidante unificado. Para función inmunológica, el mecanismo es más especulativo y descansa casi enteramente en datos de animales, creando una gran brecha inferencial desde estudios mecanísticos hasta afirmaciones de beneficio clínico.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que el efecto del extracto de ajo en presión arterial de −3,75 mmHg es clínicamente marginal (equivalente a un único cambio dietético o pérdida de peso mínima) y el intervalo de confianza es estrecho solo por la agrupación; los ECA individuales son pequeños y heterogéneos en diseño y poblaciones. Más revelador aún, si el extracto de ajo funcionara mediante un mecanismo antioxidante general o reductor de lípidos, el colesterol debería mejorar—no lo hace (IC agrupado incluye cero). La afirmación sobre función inmunológica descansa en 5 estudios en animales y 2 no clasificados; el único ECA en humanos (2006) evaluó precancerosis de lesiones gástricas, no marcadores inmunológicos. Un escéptico bien informado concluiría que la evidencia apoya una reducción de presión arterial pequeña, posiblemente clínicamente negligible, en hipertensos, sin efecto en colesterol y sin evidencia humana creíble para mejoría inmunológica.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Para presión arterial: un ECA grande (n ≥ 500), a largo plazo (≥12 semanas) en una población hipertensiva representativa con preregistro y evaluación de heterogeneidad por edad, PA basal y formulación de ajo. Para colesterol: el mismo diseño aplicado prospectivamente a afirmaciones de reducción lipídica, ya que la evidencia agrupada actual es nula. Para función inmunológica: reemplazo de la evidencia 70% en animales con ECA en humanos adecuadamente potenciados (n ≥ 200) midiendo puntos finales inmunológicos validados (p. ej., tasas de infección, respuesta de anticuerpos) en lugar de marcadores in vitro.
